list.listitem: The diagnosis of hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) in a patient with acute or chronic liver disease is based on elevated creatinine levels or reduced creatinine clearance after excluding other forms of underlying intrinsic kidney disease. C

Patients with this disorder often exhibit arterial hypotension, low urine output, low urine and serum sodium levels, elevated plasma renin activity and aldosterone levels, and elevated renal resistive index on ultrasound. C

In patients with decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, weekly albumin administration reduces risk of HRS and mortality, B and prevention of spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) in those at risk reduces the incidence and delays the onset of HRS. A
Treatment is aimed at reversing the underlying splanchnic vasodilation by using systemic vasoconstrictor therapy to reduce mortality and limit long-term renal dysfunction. A

Prognosis without liver transplant is poor and median survival is measured in weeks to months. However, short-term survival can be improved with therapy that serves as a bridge to liver transplant leading to significantly improved mortality rates. Orthotopic liver transplant is the definitive therapy. B

background.definition: Hepatorenal syndrome (HRS) is a progressive renal insufficiency occurring in patients with acute or chronic liver disease that is caused primarily by alterations in cardiovascular function. The diagnosis is based on specific diagnostic criteria after the exclusion of other forms of renal failure. Historical definitions classified type 1 HRS by an acute doubling of serum creatinine to a level of greater than 2.5 mg/dL and type 2 HRS having a slower progression with creatinine levels ranging from 1.5 to 2.5 mg/dL. Since 2015, the criteria now focus on absolute increases in creatinine above baseline levels with acute kidney injury (AKI) stages 1, 2, and 3 being identified by rises in creatinine of 1.5-times baseline, 2-3-times baseline, and greater than 3-times baseline, respectively ().

list.listitem: The incidence of hepatorenal syndrome with acute kidney injury (HRS-AKI) in patients with cirrhosis, ascites, and normal baseline renal function is 18% at 1 year and 39% at 5 years.
The 1-year incidence rate among patients with ascites was confirmed in a case series of 112 patients with liver cirrhosis of whom 20.5% developed HRS.
About one third of patients admitted to the hospital with severe alcohol-associated hepatitis have HRS.
In a study of 12,671 hospital admissions for complications of cirrhosis, hepatorenal syndrome conveyed the highest risk for death (49.2%; OR 8.1; 95% CI 6.6-9.9).
HRS occurs without an identifiable precipitating factor in up to 50% of patients.

The remainder of cases can be attributed to one or more of the following: spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) or other bacterial infection (48%), gastrointestinal bleeding (33%), excessive paracentesis (27%), and the overuse of diuretic medications (7%).

Despite theoretical concerns for inducing arterial hypotension and reducing organ perfusion, authors of a meta-analysis determined that use of non-selective beta blockers in advanced cirrhosis does not increase the risk of HRS.

The underlying mechanism for HRS is massive peripheral arterial vasodilation, particularly in the splanchnic circulation; these vasodilators include nitric oxide, carbon monoxide, prostacyclins, and endocannabinoids which cause vascular underfilling and an increase in cardiac output. The responsive increase in renin-aldosterone activity leads to renal arterial vasoconstriction and renal insufficiency.

Several other hypotheses have been forwarded to explain HRS. One hypothesis is that the vascular bed vasodilation in cirrhosis could be a consequence of blood shunting from the portal to the systemic circulations rather than a cause of volume overload. A second hypothesis is that there is a direct interaction between the liver and kidneys responsible for volume overload.

In addition, ammonia levels increase in patients with cirrhosis which disrupts arginine metabolism, reducing nitric oxide levels in the renal microcirculation and impairing renal blood flow. Systemic inflammation, with release of proinflammatory cytokines, may also contribute.
Relative adrenal insufficiency is present in up to 47% of patients with decompensated cirrhosis and may contribute to HRS; adrenal insufficiency is a risk factor for short-term mortality.

Risk_Factor.Risk_Name: Bacterial infection, especially spontaneous bacterial peritonitis

list.listitem: Direct measurement of creatinine clearance is recommended to determine true renal function in patients with cirrhosis. For patients with HRS who do not meet criteria for HRS-AKI, termed HRS-nonAKI, glomerular filtration rate is used to further classify patients as having acute or chronic kidney disease (). C
In patients with decompensated cirrhosis with ascites, long-term weekly albumin administration reduces risk of HRS and mortality. B
Antibiotic prophylaxis against spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP) reduces the incidence and delays the onset of HRS. A
Patients with alcoholic hepatitis should receive pentoxifylline, 400 mg by mouth 3 times daily, to prevent HRS. A

Prophylaxis against SBP with norfloxacin 400 mg by mouth daily reduces the incidence and delays the onset of HRS, presumably by decreasing the translocation of gut bacteria into the systemic circulation leading to improved circulatory function. A

The American Gastroenterological Association (AGA) Institute Clinical Practice 2022 Update on the clinical management of patients with suspected AKI in patients with cirrhosis recommend the following preventive measures: (1) avoidance of potentially nephrotoxic medications (e.g., nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs), (2) avoidance of excessive or unmonitored diuretics or nonselective beta-blockade, (3) avoidance of large-volume paracentesis without albumin replacement, and (4) counseling patients to avoid alcohol use.

In an RCT of 431 patients with cirrhosis and uncomplicated ascites who were treated with anti-aldosterone drugs and furosemide, those randomized to standard medical treatment plus human albumin (40 g twice weekly for 2 weeks, and then 40 g weekly) for up to 18 months compared to standard care alone had improved overall survival (77% vs. 66%).

Antibiotic prophylaxis in patients at risk SBP likely works by decreasing the translocation of gut bacteria into the systemic circulation leading to improved circulatory function. Risk is determined by low ascitic fluid protein (<1.5 mg/dL) associated with advanced liver dysfunction (bilirubin > 3 mg/dL and Child-Turcotte-Pugh score > 9) or renal dysfunction (serum sodium <130 mEq/L, BUN > 25 mg/dL or serum creatinine >1.2 mg/dL).

In an RCT of 68 patients with cirrhosis and advanced liver failure, norfloxacin (400 mg daily) vs. placebo significantly reduced the 1-year probability of developing both SBP (7% vs. 61%) and HRS (28% vs. 41%), and improved the 3-month and one-year survival (94% vs. 62% and 60% vs. 48% respectively).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies of rifaximin prophylaxis, including 1703 patients, found a pooled OR of 0.25, 95% CI 0.13-0.50 for prevention of HRS and 0.40, 95% CI: 0.22-0.73 for prevention of SBP.
See chapter on hepatic cirrhosis and chronic liver disease for additional information on prophylaxis.

In an RCT of 68 patients with severe alcoholic hepatitis, those randomized to pentoxifylline had a lower risk of developing HRS compared to those randomized to prednisolone (0% vs. 17.6%, respectively) and fewer died at 3-months post intervention (5 vs. 12 patients, respectively).
In another RCT of 176 patients with cirrhosis and ascites, fewer patients randomized to pentoxifylline vs. placebo developed type 1 HRS at 6 months (2 vs. 10 patients).
The diagnosis of HRS is based on elevated creatinine levels or reduced creatinine clearance after excluding other forms of underlying intrinsic kidney disease. C
Arterial hypotension, low urine volume, low urine and serum sodium levels, and elevated plasma renin activity and plasma aldosterone levels support the diagnosis of HRS.
An elevated renal resistive index on renal duplex Doppler ultrasound increases the probability of developing HRS.

Differential.Differential_Features: Urinary hyaline casts, elevated urine specific gravity, improvement with intravenous fluids
History of exposure to nephrotoxic drug or radiocontrast agent
History of chronic renal insufficiency, history of hypertension or diabetes
Urinary white blood cell casts, urinary eosinophils
Urinary red blood cell casts, hematuria

list.listitem: Suspect HRS in patients with features of acute or chronic liver disease: hepatomegaly or splenomegaly; jaundice; signs of volume overload, including ascites and elevated jugular venous distention; palmar erythema; gynecomastia; spider angiomas; muscle wasting; caput medusae; or testicular atrophy.

The AGA 2022 guideline recommends assessment for use of nephrotoxic drugs, nonselective beta-blockers, radiographic contrast agents, diuretics, or lactulose; excess alcohol use; signs of infection; and symptoms of vomiting, diarrhea, hematemesis, and melena. Examination focuses on detecting infection, assessing volume status, and monitoring for hepatic and extrahepatic organ failure.
Arterial hypotension with a low mean arterial pressure is a predominant feature of HRS.
Jaundice and hepatic encephalopathy are more common in patients with HRS than in cirrhotic patients with other forms of renal disease.

Diagnostic criteria for HRS are shown in . These are separated into HRS-AKI and HRS-acute kidney disease (AKD) or HRS-chronic kidney disease (CKD). HRS-AKD refers to cases in which there is no evidence of acute injury, but renal function, as measured by glomerular filtration rate (GFR), is diminished over <3 months. HRS-CKD is a reduction in GFR below 60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for 3 or more months in the absence of other causes.
There are 3 stages of AKI, also shown in .

The sensitivity of creatinine levels for detecting renal insufficiency in patients with cirrhosis is only 18.5% because increases in body weight from ascites and relative sarcopenia make this test unreliable. Calculated GFR has an improved sensitivity of 51.8%. Therefore, the direct measurement of a 24-hour creatinine clearance is recommended to determine true renal function in patients with cirrhosis.

The AGA 2022 guideline recommends investigation of the specific type of AKI using a careful history, physical examination, blood biochemistry, urine microscopic examination, urine chemistry (Na+ and urea), selected urinary biomarkers (noted below) and renal ultrasound.

Laboratory data will usually reveal low urine volume, low urinary sodium excretion, low serum sodium, and elevated plasma renin and aldosterone levels. Urinary sodium, however, can be elevated due to diuretics which are frequently used in patients with ascites.
Cystatin C is not affected by liver dysfunction and may be a more reliable method of assessing GFR in patients with cirrhosis.

Neutrophil gelatinase-associated lipocalcin (NGAL) and interleukin-18 are novel markers for renal dysfunction that may have future utility in distinguishing HRS from other forms of AKI in cirrhosis such as acute tubular necrosis. Urinary NGAL, at a cutoff value of 220 μg/g of creatinine after a fluid challenge, has the highest diagnostic accuracy for acute tubular necrosis of biomarkers tested, and appears to be a predictor of short-term mortality.

Patients with HRS also have higher D-dimer than those with the other types of AKI. In a cohort study of 773 patients with cirrhosis, using a cutoff of 3.7 mg/L FEU, sensitivity of D-Dimer for predicting development of HRS was 87.3% and specificity 72.9%, with an area under the ROC curve of 0.879 (95%CI 0.791-0.967).
Calculation of the renal resistive index by renal duplex Doppler ultrasound is recommended in patients with cirrhosis. Patients with an elevated resistive index have a 26% risk of developing HRS.
AGA 2022 guidelines also recommend a rigorous search for infection including a diagnostic paracentesis for SBP, blood and urine cultures, and chest radiograph.
See algorithm in .

Therapy with intravenous vasoconstrictors (eg, terlipressin, noradrenalin, or midodrine and octreotide) improves the rate of resolution of HRS and improves short-term survival compared with albumin alone. A Based on a comparative effectiveness review, terlipressin may be the best first-line agent, A followed by initial norepinephrine administration, with midodrine+octreotide as least effective. B
Traditional hemodialysis and/or albumin dialysis may improve short-term survival and serve as a bridge to transplant. B
Orthotopic liver transplant significantly improves survival rates in patients with HRS. B
Therapy with IV vasoconstrictors (eg, terlipressin, noradrenalin, or midodrine and octreotide) improves the rate of resolution of HRS and improves short-term survival compared with albumin alone.

Authors of a comparative effectiveness review and meta-analysis of 26 RCTs including 1,736 patients with HRS concluded that terlipressin is the best first-line agent based on high certainty of increased HRS reversal over placebo (142 reversals per 1,000, 95% CI 87.7 to 210.9) and low certainty-evidence supporting reduced mortality vs. placebo (93.7 fewer deaths, 95% CI 168.7 to 12.5). If unavailable, these authors suggest initial norepinephrine administration (112.7 reversals per 1,000, 95% CI 52.6 to 192.3; low certainty). Midodrine+octreotide was determined to be least effective (67.8 reversals per 1,000, 95% CI 2.8 to 177.4; very low certainty evidence).
Terlipressin, a vasopressin analogue, has now been FDA approved for use in hospitalized patients with type 1 HRS (HRS-AKI).

The 2022 AGA guidelines recommend treatment of HRS-AKI with albumin at 1 g/kg intravenously on day 1 followed by 20-40 g daily along with terlipressin, if available and the patient’s serum creatinine is <5 mg/dL and oxygen saturation is >90%. Terlipressin is initiated either as a bolus of 1 mg every 4-6 hours (total 4-6 mg/d) or by continuous intravenous infusion at a lower starting dose of 2 mg/d and increased gradually every 24-48 hours up to a maximum dose of 12 mg/d, or reversal of HRS; the latter approach may reduce ischemic side effects. If using bolus administration, the dose should be increased to a maximum of 2 mg every 4-6 hours (total 8-12 mg/d) if there is no reduction in serum creatinine at day 3 of therapy by at least 25% compared to the baseline value.

Adverse effects reported in the CONFIRM trial include abdominal pain, nausea, diarrhea, and respiratory failure; the latter resulted in death within 90 days in 22 patients (11%) in the terlipressin group vs. 2 patients (2%) in the placebo group. The AGA also notes adverse effects from ischemia including angina and ischemia of fingers, skin, and intestine. In a post-hoc analysis of this trial data, those with higher grades of advanced acute-on-chronic liver failure and those with hypoxemia were at greater risk for respiratory failure.
Albumin combined with terlipressin, a vasopressin analogue, leads to recovery of renal function in 43.5% of patients compared with 8.7% of patients treated with albumin alone (NNT = 3).

Based on a Cochrane review of 9 RCTs (all with high risk of bias), mortality in type 1 HRS with terlipressin therapy compared with control therapies (RR 0.85, 95% CI 0.73 to 0.98); and, in combination with albumin, has a beneficial effect on reversal of HRS (RR 0.63, 95% CI 0.48 to 0.82; 510 participants; 8 RCTs; NNT = 4 people; low‐quality evidence). Doses larger than 3 mg per day may lead to improved survival.

In the CONFIRM RCT of 300 adults with type 1 HRS, terlipressin with albumin reversed HRS in more patients (32% vs. 17% in the placebo group), but more adverse events occurred in the intervention group including death within 90 days due to respiratory disorders which occurred in 22 patients (11%) in the terlipressin group and 2 patients (2%) in the placebo group.
Preoperative treatment with terlipressin plus albumin may improve survival following liver transplantation.

Terlipressin was approved by the FDA in September 2022 for treatment of adults hospitalized with hepatorenal syndrome with rapid reduction in kidney function (HRS-1 or HRS-AKI). Approval in the U.S. was based primarily on the results of the above CONFIRM trial.

The eTerli study evaluated whether early vs standard initiation of terlipressin improved renal outcomes by day 7. The treatment arm (early administration) saw an improvement in renal function by day 3 (31.4% vs 11.4%) and had a full AKI response by day 7 (68.6% vs 31.4%). The intervention group also saw an improvement in mean arterial pressure and urine output by day 3 and needed less albumin administration within 7 days. Additionally, there was a 28-day mortality benefit in the treatment arm (40% vs 65.7%).

Terlipression treatment does not require intensive care monitoring and can be safely administered intravenously through a peripheral line. Terlipressin is contraindicated in patients who have hypoxemia or a vaso-occlusive crisis such as coronary, peripheral or mesenteric ischemia.

The AGA 2022 guidelines recommend that norepinephrine be administered as a continuous intravenous infusion at a starting dose of 0.5 mg/h. The dose is increased every 4 hours by 0.5 mg/h to a maximum of 3 mg/h with a goal of increasing the mean arterial pressure by ≥10 mm Hg and/or the urine output to >50 mL/h for at least 4 hours. The risks of ischemic side effects (e.g., angina and ischemia of fingers, skin, and intestine) may be reduced by starting at the lowest dose and gradually titrating upward.

Noradrenalin is a less expensive and more readily available alternative for HRS. When compared with terlipressin and albumin, noradrenalin and albumin are similar in achieving a complete resolution of renal dysfunction, although those on terlipressin had a higher rate of adverse events (25.4% vs. 10.6%). The most common adverse events include abdominal pain, diarrhea, and cardiac events including arrythmias.

However, in an open-label RCT of 120 consecutive patients with HRS-AKI, more patients randomized to terlipressin vs. noradrenalin experienced reversal of HRS (40% vs. 16.7%, respectively), reduced requirement for renal replacement therapy (56.6% vs. 80%) and had improved 28-day survival (48.3% vs. 20%). Adverse events were higher with terlipressin than noradrenaline (23.3% vs. 8.3%, respectively).
Based on a meta-analysis of small 13 RCTs, noradrenalin and terlipressin were more effective than midodrine plus octreotide with albumin for reversal of HRS.

Based on a systematic review and network meta-analysis of 26 RCTs, terlipressin increases HRS reversal compared to placebo (142 per 1000, 95% CI 87.7 to >210.9). Norepinephrine was also found to be effective at HRS reversal at 112.7 per 100 (95% CI 52.6 to >192.3). Midodrine plus octreotide were least effective at HRS reversal (67.8 per 1000, 95% CI <2.8 to >177.4). One noteworthy take away was that terlipressin was associated with probable increase risk of serious adverse events compared to placebo. While terlipressin may reduce mortality, norepinephrine serves as a reasonable first-line therapy over midodrine plus octreotide until terlipressin becomes more readily available.

The AGA 2022 guidelines recommend administration of oral midodrine initiated at 7.5 mg and titrated upward to 12.5 mg 3 times daily with octreotide starting with 100 μg and titrating upward to 200 μg subcutaneously 3 times daily.
Treatment with midodrine, octreotide, and albumin improves renal function in 40% of patients (compared with 10% with albumin alone) and leads to a lower 30-day mortality rate (43% vs. 71%; NNT = 3).
For patients with tense ascites, paracentesis with intravenous albumin improves hemodynamics, creatinine clearance, and urine output.

Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt (TIPS) is an alternative for patients who are not eligible for transplantation. After receiving a TIPS, 57% of patients can stop hemodialysis. In patients with refractory ascites, TIPS, as opposed to large volume paracentesis, has a positive effect on renal function in HRS and may improve survival. However, TIPS is associated with an increased frequency and severity of episodes of hepatic encephalopathy. The AGA 2022 guidelines do not recommend use of TIPS as a specific treatment of HRS-AKI.

Orthotopic liver transplant improves survival in patients with HRS with an overall reversal rate of 83%. Patients with type 1 HRS have slightly worse outcomes with complete resolution in 60% of patients. Fewer than 25% of patients require hemodialysis after transplant with livers from older donors carrying a slightly higher risk of persistent renal dysfunction. At five years post-transplant, 6-16% of patients have ongoing CKD. AGA 2022 guidelines support use of liver transplantation as the most effective treatment for HRS-AKI.

Combined liver and kidney transplantation is not recommended for patients with hepatorenal syndrome as there is no difference in survival when compared with patients receiving a liver transplant alone. Other authors, though, disagree and believe that patients with HRS who require renal replacement therapy for more than 8 to 12 weeks are good candidates for combined transplant.

For patients with AKI, AGA 2022 guidelines recommend that diuretics and nonselective beta-blockers be withheld, NSAIDs discontinued, the precipitating cause of AKI treated, and fluid losses replaced, administering albumin 1 g/kg/d for 2 days if the serum creatinine shows doubling from baseline.
Patients should continue to follow a low-sodium, fluid-restricted diet.
As renal function worsens, dietary potassium and phosphorus should be reduced to lessen the risk of electrolyte imbalance.

Renal replacement therapy (RRT) replaces the normal blood filtering kidney function with filtering to remove fluid and replace solutes through techniques including continuous hemofiltration and hemodialysis, intermittent hemodialysis, and peritoneal dialysis. AGA 2022 guidelines recommend use of RRT in patients with HRS-AKI who are potential candidates for liver transplantation.

Traditional hemodialysis is used to improve short-term survival and serve as a bridge to transplant, although this leads to an increase in morbidity. Renal replacement therapy does not appear to improve long-term survival in patients with HRS.

Albumin dialysis using a molecular absorbent recirculating system (MARS) improves short-term survival compared with hemodialysis alone. The average survival for patients treated with MARS was 25.2 days vs. 4.6 days for those receiving hemodialysis.
Referrals to a hepatologist and transplant surgeon should be made with the diagnosis of HRS.
Consider a critical care consultation, as many patients with HRS will require transfer to the intensive care unit for intensive monitoring and therapy.
Consider involvement of hospice, particularly for patients not undergoing liver transplant.
Patients with type 1 HRS (HRS-AKI) have a median survival of 1 month; patients with type 2 HRS (HRS-CKD) have a median survival of 6.7 months.

Survival was assessed in a review of 14 RCTs of patients with type 1 HRS from 2002-2018. There was no difference in survival over time, with a pooled survival rate of 34.6% (95% CI 26.4–43.8%). Study duration ranged between 7 and 180 days.

A higher Model for End-stage Liver Disease score (MELD score) is associated with lower survival rates in HRS. However, patients with a diagnosis of HRS have a worse prognosis than patients without HRS, even when matched for MELD score.
Patients with underlying alcoholic liver disease and those who require hemodialysis after liver transplantation are less likely to return to normal renal function.

Patients who respond to vasoconstrictor therapy with an increase in mean arterial pressure (MAP) of more than 10 mmHg have better survival. In another study of patients with type 1 HRS, achievement of an increase in MAP of >10 mmHg using a combination of vasoconstrictors and albumin was associated with better overall survival and transplant-free survival. Increased MAP to >15 mmHg did not result in further improvement in clinical outcome.
In one RCT including 184 patients with HRS, a reduction in AKI stage (), independent of HRS reversal, improved 90-day survival in patients.

Outcomes of liver transplant appear less favorable for patients with hepatorenal syndrome. In one case series of patients undergoing living donor liver transplantation, the 33 patients with type 1 HRS vs. the 71 with other diagnoses had significantly more preoperative intensive care unit (ICU) admissions (84.8% vs. 60.6%), more hemodialysis (48.5% vs. 0%), longer postoperative ICU stays (8 vs. 4 days), and poorer overall survival. However, 5-year survival was still nearly 80%.

cell.label: Is the absolute creatinine value increased by >0.3mg/dL?
Is creatinine relatively increased more than 1.5 times baseline value?
Continue therapy for liver disease and intermittently monitor renal function.
Ask about nephrotoxic drugs and history of CKD. Signs of hypovolemia? Check urine for protein, casts, sodium and consider trial of IV fluids. Underlying cause identified?

Is the diagnosis consistent with hepatorenal syndrome (ie, arterial hypotension, low urine and serum sodium, elevated plasma renin and aldosterone levels, high renal resistive index on duplex Doppler ultrasound)?

Begin treatment for hepatorenal syndrome: IV albumin; vasoconstrictors (midodrine + octreotide, noradrenaline, or terlipressin); consider paracentesis, TIPS, hemodialysis, and/or MARS; refer for emergent liver transplant evaluation.
Treat underlying cause of renal insufficiency.

feature.caption: Diagnostic Criteria for Hepatorenal Syndrome and Related Renal Impairment and Acute Kidney Injury.
feature.feature_body:
Diagnostic Criteria HRS-AKI Diagnostic Criteria HRS-AKD/CKD Stages of AKI
Cirrhosis with ascites HRS-AKD (nonacute injury) Stage 1
AKI (based on ICA-AKI criteria) Estimated GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for <3 months in absence of other causes Increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dl (26.5 µmol/L) OR increase in serum creatinine ≥1.5-fold to 2-fold from baseline
Increase in serum creatinine ≥0.3 mg/dl (≥26.5 µmol/L) within 48 hours, OR A percentage increase serum creatinine ≥1.5 times from baseline (within previous 3 months or prior 7 days)
Percentage increase serum creatinine ≥1.5 times from baseline (last available within 3 months)
HRS-CKD Stage 2
No response after 2 consecutive days of diuretic withdrawal and plasma volume expansion with albumin 1 g/kg/day Estimated GFR <60 ml/min/1.73 m2 for ≥3 months in absence of other causes Increase in serum creatinine >2-fold to 3-fold from baseline
Absence of shock
Stage 3
No current or recent use of nephrotoxic drugs (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, iodinated contrast media, etc.)
Increase of serum creatinine >3-fold from baseline OR serum creatinine ≥4.0 mg/dl (353.6 µmol/L) with an acute increase ≥0.3 mg/dl (26.5 µmol/L) OR initiation of renal replacement therapy
No signs of structural kidney injury (absence of proteinuria (>500 mg/day), absence of microscopic hematuria (<50 RBCs/high power field), normal renal ultrasound)
Abbreviations: AKD, acute kidney disease; AKI, acute kidney injury; CKD, chronic kidney disease; GFR, glomerular filtration rate; HRS, hepatorenal syndrome; ICA, international Club of Ascites Information from: Angeli P, Gines P, Wong F, et al. Diagnosis and management of acute kidney injury in patients with cirrhosis: Revised consensus recommendations of the International Club of Ascites.
